sentence: The ship of Theseus puts pressure on identity over time through a different route. Replace the planks one by one, and you have a ship continuous in form; reassemble the discarded planks, and you have a ship continuous in matter. Both have a claim to be the original. The case suggests that our concept of identity is not equipped to deliver a unique answer when continuity of form and of matter come apart.

One repair adds a no-false-grounds condition: knowledge is justified true belief not essentially based on any falsehood. This handles inferential Gettier cases but founders on cases where no false premise is involved, where the believer looks at a real barn but is surrounded by fakes. The luck is environmental, not inferential, so the fix is incomplete.

The dominant-kind view holds that there is, after all, just one object here, and that the apparent two are one thing falling under two sortals. Whether it can survive squashing depends on which sortal is in question. This dissolves the puzzle by relativizing persistence to a kind, but at the cost of saying that the bare object, considered apart from any sortal, has no persistence conditions of its own.

Contextualists propose that 'know' shifts its standards with conversational context. In ordinary contexts, 'I know there is a hand' is true; once the vat is mentioned, the standards rise and the same sentence becomes false. Both the skeptic and common sense are then correct, each in their own context. The cost is that knowledge attributions lose a fixed standard, which some find too high a price for peace.

Consider the hypothesis that you are a brain in a vat, fed precisely the experiences you now have. By construction, every sensory datum is consistent with both this scenario and the ordinary one. If your evidence cannot discriminate between them, then it cannot, on the face of it, justify your belief that there is a hand before you. The skeptical argument needs only this: knowledge requires ruling out the relevant alternatives, and you cannot rule this one out.

Names are arguably rigid designators: a name picks out the same individual in every possible world in which that individual exists. A definite description need not be rigid, since who satisfies it varies across worlds. This explains why 'Aristotle might not have been a philosopher' is true while 'the philosopher who taught Alexander might not have been a philosopher' is, on one reading, false.

The skeptic need not claim that we are deceived, only that we cannot rule deception out. This is a modest premise with an immodest consequence. It suggests that the gap between experience and world, once opened, cannot be closed by experience, since any further experience falls on the near side of the gap. The structure of the problem, not any particular doubt, does the damage.

There is a question whether a text can be better understood than its author understood it. The author may not have grasped all the implications, the tensions, the resonances of the work. If understanding can outstrip the author's self-understanding, then the meaning of a text is not a finished thing deposited once, but something that unfolds in the history of its reception.

subtopic: the categorical imperative and moral law
sentence: A standing objection charges the categorical imperative with formalism: a bare consistency test, critics say, cannot generate substantive duties, and many maxims can be tweaked to slip past the universalizability check. Kantians reply that the test must be applied to maxims described at the right level of generality, and that doing so is itself a substantive exercise of practical judgment, not a mechanical procedure.

The deepest question is whether the problem of universals is a discovery about the world or a choice about how to describe it. Realists treat the existence of universals as a substantive fact; some deflationists suspect the whole dispute trades on taking the grammar of predication too seriously, mistaking a feature of language for a feature of reality.

The interest theory holds that a right protects an interest important enough to justify holding others under a duty. To have a right to bodily security is for one's interest in not being harmed to be weighty enough to ground others' obligations. The objection is that some rights, such as a competent adult's right to refuse beneficial treatment, seem to protect choices that run against the holder's interests.

Twin Earth shows that meaning is not in the head. On a planet where the watery stuff is not H2O but a different compound, a speaker's word for it does not mean what 'water' means here, even if the two speakers are internally identical. The reference of natural-kind terms is fixed in part by the actual substance, so meaning depends on the environment.

Defenders reply that not all intuitions are equal. Some are fleeting and easily shaken; others are robust, surviving reflection, recurring across formulations, and cohering with our other considered judgments. The proper response to the variability findings is not to abandon intuition but to filter it, attending to the stable verdicts of careful judges rather than to snap reactions.

Neutral monism posits that mind and matter are two aspects of a single underlying stuff that is in itself neither. This promises to honor both the unity and the duality, but the promise is empty unless something can be said about the neutral base. If the base is characterized only as that which appears mentally and physically, the view risks being a label for the problem rather than a solution to it.

Causal accounts hold that to explain an event is to cite its causes, to locate it in the causal structure of the world. This handles the asymmetry, since causes explain effects and not the reverse. But mathematical explanations and explanations of statistical regularities seem not to be causal, suggesting that explanation is broader than causation, or that there are several distinct explanatory relations.

Consider a thought that has no real object, such as the dread of a danger that does not exist. Intentionality cannot then be a relation to an existing thing, since one of the relata is missing. This pushes some toward holding that intentional objects are intrinsic contents of the act rather than external items, and the act carries its object within itself even when nothing answers to it.

A theory of distributive justice must say how the benefits and burdens of social cooperation should be shared. Goods do not fall from the sky already labeled; they are produced together and divided by institutions. The question is by what principle: equal shares, shares proportioned to need, to desert, to contribution, or shares set by whatever free exchanges people happen to make.

Defeaters complicate any account of justification. A justified belief can lose its standing when new information undermines it, either by directly opposing its content or by impugning the source of its support. A satisfactory theory must explain not only how beliefs become justified but how justification, once had, can be lost, and what makes a piece of information a genuine defeater rather than mere noise.

If the B-theory is correct, the felt passage of time demands explanation as a feature of experience rather than of the world. Perhaps the impression of flow arises from the way memory accumulates and consciousness updates. The challenge is to explain the vividness of becoming without granting it any place in the temporal structure of reality itself.

subtopic: the categorical imperative and moral law
sentence: Autonomy, for Kant, is the property of the will of being a law to itself. The moral law is not imposed from outside, by God, nature, or society, but is the law a rational will gives itself. This is why obeying it is freedom rather than constraint: in following the categorical imperative the agent is governed by her own rational nature rather than by alien forces.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: The loop variant pressures the means-versus-side-effect line. Suppose the diverted track loops back, so the trolley would still hit the five unless the one body on the side track stops it. Now the one death is a means even in the diversion case, yet many still find diversion permissible. If intuition does not track the intended-or-foreseen distinction here, the distinction may not be doing the explanatory work claimed for it.

One might distinguish the badness of being dead from the badness of dying. Dying can involve pain, fear, and loss of dignity, all straightforwardly bad experiences. Being dead, by contrast, involves no experience at all, and it is here that the Epicurean challenge bites. Much ordinary fear of death may really be fear of dying, which the Epicurean argument leaves wholly untouched.

subtopic: the is-ought problem and the grounds of value
sentence: The gap may bear on the relation between science and ethics. If no description of human nature, however thorough, entails a conclusion about how we ought to live, then ethics cannot simply be read off biology or psychology. The sciences may inform ethics by telling us what is possible and what the effects of our choices are, but the evaluative premises must come from elsewhere.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: The doctrine of double effect distinguishes harm intended as a means from harm merely foreseen as a side effect. Diverting the trolley foresees the one death; pushing the man uses his death as the means of stopping the trolley. If intention bears moral weight, the cases come apart. But it is strange that the same outcome, brought about by the same agent for the same reason, should differ in permissibility merely by how it figures in a plan.

Cultural relativism observes that moral codes vary widely across societies and concludes that there is no standard above the codes by which any could be judged. What is right is what a given culture approves. The objection is that the variety of codes is a fact about belief, and from variety in belief nothing follows about whether there is a truth those beliefs are getting more or less right.

Constructivism offers a middle path: moral truths are not discovered in a mind-independent order, nor are they mere expressions of feeling, but are the outputs of an idealized procedure of practical reasoning. What is right is what agents would agree to under suitably fair conditions. Whether this counts as realism depends on whether the procedure tracks an independent truth or constitutes the truth it yields.

subtopic: the self and the unity of consciousness
sentence: If the self is a fiction, the fiction is a peculiarly insistent one. The sense of being a single subject persisting through time, the owner of one's thoughts, is not easily dislodged by argument. A theory that denies the self must therefore explain why the illusion is so robust, and an explanation of so deep an appearance is itself a substantial task.

subtopic: the limits of language and the unsayable
sentence: Qualitative experience seems to strain language. I can describe the causes and effects of seeing red, but the felt quality itself I can only point to, trusting that you have something similar. If the intrinsic character of experience cannot be conveyed but only invoked in one who already has it, then there is a meaningful aspect of reality that escapes communication.

Fictional discourse pressures ontological commitment. We say that Sherlock Holmes is a detective and that he does not exist, apparently both truly. Either there are nonexistent objects to bear such properties, or the truths about fiction must be paraphrased so that no commitment to Holmes survives, perhaps as truths about a story rather than about a man.

subtopic: logic and the foundations of inference
sentence: Are the laws of logic descriptive, normative, or constitutive? They are not generalizations about how people reason, since people reason badly. They seem to say how one ought to reason. But a mere norm could be flouted, whereas the laws of logic seem to be the conditions under which thought is thought at all, which suggests they are constitutive rather than merely prescriptive.

Aesthetic experience is sometimes said to require disinterest, an attention to the object freed from desire and use. The thing is contemplated for its own sake. Critics charge that no perception is so pure, that we always bring concepts and interests, and that the demand for disinterest empties aesthetic experience of exactly the human concerns that make art matter.

Suppose we map every neural correlate of pain with perfect precision. We would still face an explanatory residue: why is there something it is like to be in pain at all? The functional story explains discrimination, avoidance, and report, but it leaves the qualitative felt character untouched. This is the gap that no amount of additional structural detail seems to close, and it is not obvious that calling it an illusion dissolves it rather than renaming it.

subtopic: logic and the foundations of inference
sentence: Logical truth seems necessary, knowable without experience, and general. Explaining this trio is hard. If logical truths are true by convention, conventions could have been otherwise, threatening necessity. If they describe a realm of logical facts, knowing them a priori becomes mysterious. The status of logic, the very framework of inquiry, is itself a contested philosophical question.

Whether an animal has moral status turns in part on whether it has a mind, and in particular whether it can suffer. If a creature can feel pain, then there is something it is like to be that creature, and its pain is bad for it in a way that makes a claim on us. The question of animal minds is thus not idle curiosity but the hinge of a moral question.

Quine proposed a criterion of ontological commitment: a theory is committed to whatever its variables must range over for its claims to be true. To be is to be the value of a bound variable. This turns ontology into a question about the regimented logical form of our best theories, and what we must quantify over once they are made precise.

subtopic: determinism, chance, and the open future
sentence: Fatalism is sometimes confused with determinism but is a distinct and stranger thesis. Logical fatalism argues that since it is now either true or false that a sea battle will occur tomorrow, the matter is already settled, regardless of any causal process. The flaw, most hold, lies in sliding from the timeless truth of a statement to the fixedness, by necessity, of what it describes.

Virtue ethics asks not which acts are right but what kind of person one should be. The right action is what the virtuous person would do, where virtue is a stable disposition to feel, perceive, and act well. This relocates the primary object of moral assessment from discrete choices to enduring character, and it makes moral knowledge a matter of practical wisdom rather than of applying a rule.

Reference may be partly indeterminate. The causal chain behind a term, the descriptions in circulation, and the speaker's intentions may not jointly single out a unique object, leaving it unsettled exactly what is being talked about. If reference is sometimes vague or divided, then so is the content of our thoughts, and the world we describe is described less sharply than we suppose.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: One might distrust the whole method. Trolley cases are bizarre, and intuitions tuned by ordinary life may simply not transfer to them. If the cases are too unlike anything we evolved or were trained to handle, our verdicts about them carry little evidential weight, and building moral theory on them is building on sand.

subtopic: power, ideology, and the critique of reason
sentence: The genealogical method asks not whether a value or a concept is true but how it came to be, what struggles and interests gave rise to it. By exposing the contingent, often disreputable origins of what is taken as timeless, genealogy aims to loosen the grip of the present arrangement. Its critics ask whether tracing an origin can settle anything about validity.

subtopic: determinism, chance, and the open future
sentence: Whether the universe is deterministic is, in part, an empirical question, to be informed by physics. But what would follow for freedom, responsibility, and the meaning of deliberation does not read straight off the physics. The bearing of the scientific answer on the human questions is itself a matter of philosophical argument, and the two should not be collapsed.

subtopic: the self and the unity of consciousness
sentence: The unity of consciousness across time poses a different problem than its unity at a moment. The experience I have now is connected to the one I had a moment ago by memory and by a felt continuity, but this is a relation among experiences, not the persistence of an experiencer alongside them. Whether diachronic unity needs a persisting subject, or only the right relations, is the heart of the dispute.

Rights can conflict, and when they do, the picture of rights as absolute trumps comes under pressure. If your right to free expression collides with another's right not to be defamed, at least one right must yield. This suggests rights are not exceptionless but have an internal structure, with scope conditions and weights, that determines how they are specified when they meet.

The counterfactual analysis proposes that c caused e when, had c not occurred, e would not have occurred. This captures the difference between causes and mere correlates and explains why we cite the spark rather than the oxygen. But it stumbles on cases of redundant causation, where a backup cause would have produced the effect anyway, so the counterfactual fails though the cause is real.

If every event, including every decision, follows necessarily from prior causes obeying fixed laws, then no agent could have done otherwise in the precise circumstances that obtained. The incompatibilist concludes that determinism rules out the freedom required for responsibility. The compatibilist replies that the relevant freedom is not the power to violate causation but the power to act on one's own desires unimpeded, and determinism poses no threat to that.

subtopic: determinism, chance, and the open future
sentence: Indeterminism is sometimes invoked to rescue human freedom, on the thought that a determined act could not be free. But undetermined need not mean controlled. An act that issues from a random swerve is not thereby up to the agent; it is merely uncaused, or chancy. The mere absence of determination does not by itself supply the kind of authorship that freedom seems to require.

There is a difference between holding that animals have moral status and holding that they have rights. Status implies that their interests must be weighed; rights would imply that certain treatment of them is forbidden whatever the gain. One can grant that an animal's suffering counts while denying it the kind of inviolability that rights confer, and the choice between these has large practical consequences.

The relation between wisdom and happiness is contested. The ancient view tied them tightly: the wise person, seeing things as they are and ordering their desires accordingly, is thereby the one who lives well and is least at the mercy of fortune. A more pessimistic strand suspects that seeing clearly can darken a life, that some illusions are kind, and that wisdom and contentment may pull apart.

The underdetermination thesis holds that for any body of evidence, more than one theory can fit it, so evidence cannot single out a unique truth. If genuine rivals always exist, belief in any particular theory is unwarranted. The realist replies that the alleged rivals are often gerrymandered, not serious competitors, and that explanatory virtues break the tie that mere evidence leaves open.

The distinction between de dicto and de re modality matters here. To say it is necessary that the number of planets is even differs from saying of the number of planets that it is necessarily even. The first concerns a proposition; the second attributes a modal property to an object. Possible-worlds semantics renders the difference as a difference in the scope of the modal operator.

subtopic: the is-ought problem and the grounds of value
sentence: Suppose nothing grounds value, that there is no fact, no rational structure, and no attitude that ultimately underwrites our oughts. The conclusion would not be that some things ought to be done and others not; it would be that ought-claims, all of them, fail to hit anything. Whether that nihilist possibility is coherent, and whether it could be lived, is the deepest stake in the question of value's grounds.

A thought experiment can do real work even without yielding a verdict to be tallied. It can make a possibility vivid, isolate a variable, or expose a hidden assumption. The trolley cases earn their place not merely by eliciting reactions but by holding the consequences fixed and varying the manner of harm, so that whatever explains the difference must be the manner itself.

Trans-world identity asks whether the very same individual exists across worlds. Could Caesar himself have been a baker? If individuals are world-bound, the question is malformed. Counterpart theory answers that what is true of Caesar in another world is true of his counterpart there, a distinct individual who resembles him most. This makes modal claims about individuals oddly comparative.

Process theories locate causation in physical processes that transmit something, a conserved quantity, from cause to effect. A genuine causal process can carry a mark; a pseudo-process, like a shadow's motion, cannot. This grounds causation in physics rather than in counterfactuals. Its limit is causation by absence: the gardener's failure to water caused the plant's death, yet no quantity was transmitted by a non-event.

To examine one's life is to risk discovering that one has been living it badly, and this is why the examined life is demanding rather than merely pleasant. Self-examination can dislodge cherished beliefs, expose self-deception, and unsettle a comfortable self-image. The value claimed for it must therefore be a value worth that disturbance, the value of living in the truth rather than in a flattering fiction.

Whatever principle one favors, a question of scope remains: is justice a virtue only of institutions, the basic structure of society, or does it govern individual choices as well? If the basic structure is just, may individuals within it pursue self-interest freely, or does justice make demands on their daily decisions too? The answer shapes how heavy the demands of justice fall on a life.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: Modest foundationalism weakens the classic claim: basic beliefs need not be infallible, only justified to some degree without resting on other beliefs, and that justification can be defeated by further evidence. This is more plausible than the incorrigible-foundations picture, but it must explain how a non-inferential belief gets any positive justification at all if not from another belief.

Grue dramatizes the trouble. Define grue as observed-before-now-and-green, or not-so-observed-and-blue. Every observed emerald is both green and grue. The two hypotheses agree on the past and diverge for the future. Induction alone cannot tell us to project green rather than grue, so something beyond observed instances must be doing the work of selecting which predicates are projectible.

Causation by omission strains every theory. The lifeguard's failure to act caused the drowning; but failures are not events, and an infinity of others also failed to act without being blamed. Counterfactual dependence holds for all of them. What distinguishes the lifeguard's omission seems to be a normative fact about duty, which suggests our notion of cause is partly shaped by interests and norms.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: The Sellarsian dilemma sharpens the worry about the foundations. The experience that grounds a basic belief either has propositional content or it does not. If it does, it is itself the sort of thing that can be justified or unjustified, and the regress continues. If it does not, it is hard to see how something non-propositional could justify a belief, which is propositional.

Counterfactuals are naturally analyzed with worlds: 'had the match been struck, it would have lit' is true if, in the closest worlds where it is struck, it lights. This requires a similarity ordering among worlds, and specifying that ordering without circularity is delicate, since which similarities count seems itself to depend on causal and lawlike facts.

The mind seems to have features no physical thing has: thoughts are about things, experiences have a felt quality, and mental states resist location in space. Yet minds clearly depend on brains. Dualism honors the apparent difference at the cost of explaining interaction; physicalism honors the dependence at the cost of explaining the apparent difference. The problem is that each datum, difference and dependence, undermines the natural account of the other.

The lived body is not the body as the anatomist describes it. It is the body I am, the standpoint from which the world is laid out, the silent agent of my reaching and walking. I do not infer where my hand is; I simply know, in acting. The phenomenology of embodiment shows that the subject is not a mind lodged in a mechanism but a bodily being woven into a world.

The objection from separateness of persons holds that summing welfare across individuals ignores a morally crucial fact: there is no super-person who enjoys the total. A burden imposed on one is not compensated by a benefit to another, because the one who bears the burden is not the one who reaps the benefit. Aggregation makes sense within a life, where trade-offs have a single subject, but its extension across lives is what the objection challenges.

Natural evil, the suffering caused by disease, earthquake, and predation, resists the free will defense, since no creaturely choice produces it. Some extend the defense by attributing natural evil to fallen spirits; others argue that a law-governed natural order is itself a great good, and that such an order will inevitably produce suffering as a by-product its goodness does not require but cannot exclude.

Some argue that knowledge varies with practical stakes: you can know where the bank is when little hangs on it but fail to know the very same thing when much hangs on it, your evidence unchanged. If true, this pragmatic encroachment makes knowledge sensitive to interests, which is surprising if knowledge is meant to track only truth and evidence.

Gettier's cases share a structure. A justified belief is inferred from a false premise yet happens to be true, or a belief is justified and true but the justification connects to the truth only by accident. The lesson is that justification can be present while the believer's grip on the truth is fortuitous, and knowledge requires the grip to be non-accidental.

subtopic: political authority and the social contract
sentence: Rousseau located legitimacy in the general will, the will of citizens aimed at the common good rather than at private interest. To obey laws one has, as a citizen, helped to author is not subjection but freedom, since one obeys oneself. The trouble lies in identifying the general will and in the worry that, on this view, a citizen could be 'forced to be free.'

subtopic: determinism, chance, and the open future
sentence: The asymmetry of the actual past and the open future may not need a deep metaphysical ground. It may flow from the asymmetry of records and traces: the past has left a vast settled imprint that constrains belief, while the future has left none. On this deflationary view, the openness of the future is a fact about the distribution of evidence, not about the structure of time.

The conceivability of a scenario is often taken to show its possibility, and possibility claims do philosophical heavy lifting. But conceivability is a fallible guide. We can seem to conceive of things, water that is not H2O, that turn out impossible once we understand them better. The reliability of imagination as a window onto modal truth is itself a contested question.

Two apples are both red, two triangles both three-sided. They share something, and the sharing seems real, not invented. The realist concludes there exists a single entity, redness or triangularity, present in each instance. The nominalist resists positing such repeatable entities and tries to account for resemblance using only particular things. The dispute is about what the world must contain to make sameness of type possible.

Safety reverses the modal direction: you know that p only if you could not easily have believed it falsely. In nearby possible worlds where you hold the belief, it is true. Safety handles the lottery, where you cannot know your ticket will lose because you could easily believe it falsely. Whether safety can be specified without circular appeal to knowledge remains contested.

Soul-making theodicy reconceives the world not as a paradise but as a vale of soul-making, an environment of genuine hardship in which creatures can develop virtues that could not exist without challenge. Courage, compassion, and perseverance require something to overcome. On this view, a world without suffering would be a world without the conditions for the highest goods.

Sellars attacked the myth of the given: the idea that perception delivers a foundational layer of self-certifying knowledge, uncontaminated by concepts. He argued that anything that could justify a belief must itself be conceptually structured, and so cannot be a bare, theory-free given. If he is right, there is no neutral observational bedrock, and empiricism must be rebuilt without one.

Some respond not by justifying evil but by reconceiving the divine attributes. If God is not omnipotent in the absolute sense, but works with the resistance of a partly recalcitrant creation, the problem softens, since God prevents what God can. The cost is a smaller deity, and the question whether such a being is the one the tradition meant to affirm.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: Ask why you believe something, and you cite a reason; ask why you believe the reason, and you cite another. This chain cannot go back forever, cannot loop, and cannot simply stop without warrant, or so it seems. The regress argument forces a choice among infinitism, coherentism, and foundationalism, and each option has long been thought to face decisive objections.

subtopic: the limits of language and the unsayable
sentence: Some have argued that the deepest philosophical problems arise when language idles, when words are used apart from the contexts that give them sense. The cure for such problems is not a theory but a return of words to their everyday use. On this view philosophy does not discover an unsayable truth; it dissolves the confusions that made an unsayable truth seem necessary.

The situationist challenge draws on experiments suggesting behavior depends heavily on trivial situational factors rather than on robust traits. If finding a coin makes people markedly more helpful, perhaps there are no cross-situationally stable virtues at all. Virtue ethicists respond that full virtue is rare and demanding precisely because it is robust, and that the experiments measure ordinary unreflective dispositions, not the trained character the theory describes.

There is a question whether emotions are within our control and so subject to moral assessment. We do not seem able to feel an emotion at will, yet we hold people responsible for their anger, their envy, their lack of compassion. The resolution may be that emotions, though not directly chosen, are shaped over time by attention and habit, and it is for that shaping that we are answerable.

Does time pass, or is passage an illusion? The A-theory holds that the present is metaphysically privileged and that events genuinely become past. The B-theory holds that all times are equally real and that 'past,' 'present,' and 'future' merely mark relations to the speaker, like 'here' and 'there.' Our experience seems to side with the A-theory, but physics and logic press toward the B-theory.

We are, much of the time, dispersed into the anonymous 'they,' doing what one does, thinking what one thinks, our possibilities prescribed by no one in particular and so by everyone. This is not a moral failing but the ordinary condition of social existence. Authenticity is not escape from it but a way of taking it up, seizing one's own possibilities back from the impersonal drift.

Interpretation is constrained but not determined by the text. A reading must answer to the words, and some readings can be shown to violate them; yet within those limits more than one defensible interpretation usually remains. This places interpretation between the extremes of a single correct decoding and a free play in which any reading is as good as any other.

I never perceive a physical object all at once. The cup shows me a face, while its hidden side is co-given as a horizon of further faces I could bring into view. Perception is thus shot through with anticipation: what is present always points beyond itself. This profile structure is why a thing can be experienced as one persisting object rather than a succession of disconnected glimpses.

subtopic: the categorical imperative and moral law
sentence: The first formulation directs you to act only on a maxim you could at the same time will to be a universal law. The test is not whether universal adoption would have bad consequences, but whether the maxim could even be conceived or willed as universal without contradiction. A maxim that destroys its own point when universalized fails the test, and the action it describes is forbidden.

Some draw a more radical conclusion: that identity itself is, in certain cases, indeterminate, that it is simply not settled whether the reassembled ship is the original. Others insist that identity cannot be vague, that any vagueness must lie in our language or our concepts rather than in the world, and that the appearance of indeterminate identity is always a sign of an unclear question.

The pragmatist proposes that the true is what works, what would be agreed upon at the ideal end of inquiry. This ties truth to inquiry and to consequences. The objection is that a belief can be useful while false and useless while true, so utility cannot be what truth consists in, even if it is often a sign of it.

Psychological egoism claims that every action is ultimately motivated by self-interest, that even apparent altruism aims at the agent's own benefit, such as the avoidance of guilt or the pleasure of helping. The thesis is empirical, but it has a way of becoming unfalsifiable: any counterexample is reinterpreted as a hidden self-serving motive, and a claim immune to all evidence has explained nothing.

Hume located the standard of taste not in the object alone but in the verdict of qualified critics, those with delicacy, practice, freedom from prejudice, and good sense. Beauty is what such critics converge upon. The proposal explains how taste can be better or worse while remaining anchored in response, but it must defend the claim that the qualified critics would in fact converge.

The argument from disagreement notes that moral views vary across cultures and eras far more than scientific views do, and that moral disputes often resist resolution by evidence. The anti-realist takes this as a sign that there is no fact of the matter. The realist replies that disagreement also persists in disputed empirical and philosophical questions without showing those have no answers, and that moral disagreement may stem from non-moral error.

Platonic realism places universals in a realm of their own, outside space and time, with particulars participating in them. This explains how the same property can be wholly present in many places at once: it is not, strictly, in space at all. The price is a second realm and the obscure relation of participation, plus the question of how spatial minds grasp non-spatial forms.

subtopic: the self and the unity of consciousness
sentence: Split-brain cases trouble the assumption that one body houses one stream of consciousness. When the hemispheres are surgically divided, the two halves can be given conflicting information and respond independently, as if two centers of awareness coexisted. This suggests the unity of consciousness is not metaphysically guaranteed but depends on physical integration that can be disrupted.

The new evil demon thought experiment pressures externalism. Imagine someone whose experiences are exactly like ours but who is systematically deceived; their belief-forming processes are unreliable through no fault of theirs. Intuitively their beliefs are as justified as ours, since they are reasoning impeccably. If justification can be present without reliability, then reliability is not what justification consists in.

A semantic reply argues that if you really were a brain in a vat, your word 'vat' would not refer to vats but to features of your simulation, so the sentence 'I am a brain in a vat' would be false in your mouth. If sound, this shows the skeptical hypothesis is in a sense self-undermining. But it leaves untouched a recently envatted brain, and the worry returns in a slightly altered form.

Why be virtuous? Aristotle answers that virtue is constitutive of eudaimonia, the flourishing that is the final end of a human life. Virtue is not instrumental to a separate payoff; it is part of what living well consists in. This grounds the demands of ethics in the agent's own good, avoiding the picture of morality as an external imposition on a self that would otherwise prefer otherwise.

The conceivability of disembodied minds and of mindless bodies has long been used to argue for dualism. But conceivability arguments cut both ways and depend on a tight link between what we can imagine and what is possible. The mind-body problem may be less about which arguments win than about why our concepts of the mental and the physical resist being thought together at all.

The growing-block view splits the difference: the past and present exist, accumulating, while the future does not yet. This preserves the openness of the future and the fixity of the past. But it generates a strange epistemic problem, for if past moments are equally real, how do I know that I am at the growing edge rather than stranded in some long-elapsed now?

Deontology can accommodate the intuition that some sacrifices are heroic but not required. Constraints forbid; they do not command optimization. Within the space left by constraints, an agent has prerogatives and may pursue her own life. This gives deontology a structural advantage over maximizing theories: it explains why morality is not relentlessly demanding, because its core is a set of limits rather than a single goal.

The deepest question for deontology is what unifies the constraints. Are prohibitions on killing, lying, and promise-breaking instances of a single principle, such as respect for rational agency, or an irreducible plurality? A unified ground promises systematicity and a way to settle hard cases; a plurality may be more faithful to moral experience but leaves the theory looking like a list rather than an explanation.

Meinong notoriously allowed for objects that do not exist, such as the golden mountain and the round square, holding that we can think and speak truly about them. Russell rejected this, arguing that apparent reference to nonexistents dissolves under analysis into quantified claims that carry no such commitment. The dispute set the agenda for how language relates to ontology.

Lucretius posed the symmetry argument: we do not regret the eternity before our birth, when we also did not exist, so we should not dread the eternity after our death. The two stretches of nonexistence are alike. Resisting this requires explaining why the future void is worse than the past one, and a plausible answer appeals to the asymmetry of our concern, which is directed forward.

One response says the statue is constituted by the lump without being identical to it. Constitution is a relation tighter than mere co-location but looser than identity: the lump makes up the statue, the way a constitution can change a thing's persistence conditions. Critics ask how two distinct objects can share all their parts and all their physical properties, and yet be two.

subtopic: logic and the foundations of inference
sentence: Logical pluralism holds that there is more than one correct logic, that different consequence relations are each legitimate for different purposes or domains. Logical monism insists that one logic captures the real relation of following-from. The pluralist must explain how, if logics disagree about which inferences are valid, they can all be correct without contradiction.

Compatibilism can seem like a redefinition that changes the subject. The plain person worried about free will wants to know whether the future is genuinely open and whether they are the true author of their acts. Telling them that freedom merely means acting unconstrained by external force may answer a question, but perhaps not the one they were asking.

Constructive empiricism offers an anti-realist alternative: a good theory need only be empirically adequate, true in what it says about observables, and acceptance of a theory involves no belief about its unobservable claims. Science aims at saving the phenomena, not at truth about the hidden. The realist objects that the line between observable and unobservable is arbitrary and does not mark a real epistemic divide.

A creature could process information, model its environment, and report its states without any of that processing being accompanied by felt quality. So the question is not what consciousness does but why doing it ever feels like anything. To answer that the feeling just is the doing is to assert an identity, and an identity claim across such an explanatory chasm demands a justification we do not yet possess.

Apparent moral disagreement across cultures often dissolves on inspection into agreement on values combined with disagreement on facts. Two societies that treat the elderly very differently may share the value of respect while differing about what circumstances and beliefs make particular treatment respectful. The deep diversity relativism trades on may be shallower than it first appears.

subtopic: the is-ought problem and the grounds of value
sentence: Even if the strict logical point stands, that ought is not entailed by is alone, it does not follow that facts are irrelevant to value. Facts can ground oughts together with an evaluative premise, and they can constrain which evaluative conclusions are tenable. The is-ought problem rules out one route from fact to value; it does not show that the two domains are sealed off from each other.

Skeptical theism replies that we are in no position to judge whether a given evil is pointless. A good beyond our grasp might require it, and a finite mind cannot survey the whole web of consequences. The move blunts the evidential argument, but at a cost: if we cannot judge that any evil is gratuitous, we may also lose the ability to judge that anything is good or bad at all.

Aristotelian realism keeps universals but locates them in their instances: redness exists, but only as the redness of red things, never uninstantiated. This avoids a separate realm. It struggles, though, with universals that happen never to be instantiated, and with the claim that one and the same entity is wholly present in each of its many bearers.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: Whatever one concludes, the trolley problem exposes that our moral thought is not a single coherent algorithm. We deploy consequentialist reasoning, constraints against using people, and distinctions of intention, and these can conflict. A complete moral theory must either show one of these to be fundamental and the others derivative, or explain how they coexist without collapsing into incoherence.

The distinction between doing and allowing carries great weight for deontology. Killing is worse than letting die, even when the death is the same, because in killing you initiate a fatal sequence while in allowing you merely fail to interrupt one. Critics press cases where the distinction seems to vanish, and the deontologist must show that the line marks a genuine moral joint rather than a mere description of physical proximity.

The Quinean criterion reframes ontological dispute. To deny that numbers exist, one must show that mathematical claims, when properly paraphrased, do not require quantification over numbers. If no such paraphrase succeeds and mathematics is indispensable to science, then we are committed to numbers whether or not we find abstract objects congenial.

subtopic: the self and the unity of consciousness
sentence: Against the bundle view stands the apparent unity of consciousness at a moment. My visual field, the sound I hear, and the thought I am thinking are not three separate awarenesses running in parallel; they are had together, in a single experience. This co-consciousness seems to require something more than a collection, some unifying structure that makes many contents one consciousness.

Religious experience is offered as direct evidence: people report encounters with the divine as vivid as any sense perception. The principle of credulity says we should trust such reports absent special reason to doubt them. The skeptic notes that religious experiences conflict across traditions and lack the public checkability of sense perception, which weakens the analogy with ordinary observation.

A text can be approached with trust, seeking the truth it has to offer, or with suspicion, asking what interests and illusions it conceals. The hermeneutics of suspicion treats the surface meaning as a mask over a hidden function. Whether suspicion or trust should be primary, and whether a reading can be both, is a question about what interpretation is ultimately for.

The constitution puzzles can seem like scholastic curiosities, but they probe something basic: whether the familiar objects of common sense, statues, ships, persons, have determinate, mind-independent persistence conditions. If the answer is unclear, then the everyday world of enduring things may be, in part, a projection of our sortal concepts onto a reality that does not, on its own, come so neatly bounded.

If animals have moral status, the implications reach beyond how we treat individual creatures. They bear on agriculture, research, habitat, and the structure of economies. A philosophy that grants animals genuine standing cannot treat the conclusion as a private sentiment; it commits one to revising practices on a scale that the comfort of the conclusion's abstractness can obscure.

The correspondence theory says a belief is true when it matches the facts. The picture is intuitive but the matching relation resists analysis: what is it for a proposition to correspond to a fact, and what are facts other than whatever makes true propositions true? If facts are individuated by the propositions they verify, the theory threatens to say only that a true proposition corresponds to its being true.

Epistemic norms appear to be genuinely normative: there are beliefs one ought and ought not to hold, and a believer can be criticized for failing the standard. But belief is not typically under direct voluntary control; one cannot believe at will. If ought implies can, and one cannot simply choose what to believe, the sense in which there are duties to believe well needs careful explanation.

The capability approach shifts the focus from the distribution of resources to what people are actually able to do and to be. Two people given the same income may have very different real freedoms if one is disabled or lives where opportunities are scarce. Justice, on this view, concerns the distribution of effective freedoms, not merely of the means that imperfectly translate into them.

The pessimistic induction looks at the history of science and notes that past theories, once successful, were later judged false, their central terms found to refer to nothing. Phlogiston, caloric, and the ether enjoyed predictive success and were abandoned. By induction, our current theories will likely meet the same fate, which undercuts the inference from success to truth.

Causation comes in degrees and kinds: contributing causes, triggering causes, background conditions, enabling conditions. Ordinary causal talk selects one factor as the cause and demotes the rest to conditions, and the selection tracks our interests, what is abnormal, and what we could have controlled. A theory of causation must decide whether this selectivity is part of causation itself or a pragmatic overlay on a neutral relation.

subtopic: logic and the foundations of inference
sentence: Higher-order vagueness threatens the project of regimenting reasoning about borderline cases. Even if we admit a third category for the indeterminate, there will be borderline cases of the borderline, and so on. The boundary between the clear and the unclear is itself unclear, and no finite layering of categories seems to capture a phenomenon that resists every sharp line.

Socrates declared that the unexamined life is not worth living, a startling claim, since most lives are unexamined and their owners do not think them worthless. The claim is best read not as a verdict on others but as a standard for oneself: a life in which one never asks what one is doing and why is, for a being capable of asking, a life that falls short of itself.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: A runaway trolley will kill five unless you divert it onto a track where it will kill one. Most judge diverting permissible. Change the case: you can stop the trolley only by pushing a large stranger off a footbridge into its path, killing him to save five. Most judge this impermissible. The numbers are identical; the difference must lie in how the harm is brought about, and articulating that difference is the philosophical task.

subtopic: the limits of language and the unsayable
sentence: Poetry suggests that language can do more than state. It can enact, evoke, and bring to presence something that no paraphrase preserves. If a poem's meaning cannot be exhaustively restated in plain prose, then there is content carried by form, rhythm, and resonance, and the sayable is wider, or stranger, than the propositional model of meaning allows.

Authenticity is not a fixed achievement but a way of holding oneself, always at risk of lapsing. One can be authentic in a moment of clear self-ownership and slide back into evasion the next. This is why the existentialist treats it less as a state to reach than as a stance to renew, a continual reclaiming of a life that is never finished while it is lived.

Even if realism about a domain is warranted, the unity of science is not thereby assured. The special sciences traffic in kinds, such as species and economic classes, that do not reduce to the kinds of physics, yet they support genuine explanations. Whether these higher-level kinds are real, and how their explanations relate to the physical ones beneath, is a question realism alone does not settle.

If emotions embody evaluations, they can be correct or incorrect. Fear of a harmless thing is mistaken not merely inconvenient; it gets the world wrong. This makes emotions answerable to reasons and educable. The opposing tradition treats emotions as brute feelings, mere agitations of the body, and on that view they can be neither true nor false, only stronger or weaker.

subtopic: the is-ought problem and the grounds of value
sentence: Defenders of ethical naturalism reply that the open-question argument proves too much. It would block any informative identification, including those, like water being H2O, that are clearly true. Identity statements can be informative and a posteriori; that one can wonder whether the good is the pleasant no more refutes their identity than wondering whether water is H2O refutes that one.

Rawls proposed that just principles are those that would be chosen behind a veil of ignorance, by parties who do not know their place, talents, or conception of the good. Ignorant of how they will fare, rational choosers would not gamble with the worst-off position. The resulting principles secure equal basic liberties and permit inequalities only insofar as they benefit the least advantaged.

Natural rights are said to belong to persons simply as persons, prior to and independent of any legal recognition, in virtue of features like rational agency or the capacity for a life of one's own. Critics, following Bentham, deride this as nonsense upon stilts, holding that rights are creatures of positive law and that talk of pre-legal rights confuses what is the case with what one wishes were.

If there is no God and no given essence, then values are not discovered ready-made; they are brought into being by commitment. This does not make choice arbitrary, the existentialist insists, since in choosing for oneself one chooses a picture of how a human being should live, and so chooses, in a sense, for everyone. The weight of that responsibility is precisely what authenticity refuses to evade.

If rights are not legal artifacts, what fixes which ones exist? One answer grounds them in human dignity, in the special standing of beings capable of autonomy. Another grounds them in the conditions required for any minimally decent life. Each grounding shapes the content of the rights: an autonomy-based account foregrounds liberties, a needs-based one foregrounds welfare provisions.

subtopic: the self and the unity of consciousness
sentence: Some traditions treat the dissolution of the sense of self not as a theoretical conclusion but as an experiential possibility, reached in certain disciplined states. If the felt boundary of the self can be loosened or undone in experience, that is data: it suggests the unity of self is not a fixed given but a variable feature of consciousness, sometimes present in a different mode and sometimes seemingly absent.

If moral relativism were true, then no culture's practices could be criticized from outside, and a reformer who condemns her own society's accepted practice would simply be mistaken, since the practice is, by hypothesis, right for that society. Relativism thus makes moral reform unintelligible as anything but error, which is a heavy and counterintuitive consequence to accept.

There is a recurring tension between two pictures of justification. On the internalist picture, what justifies a belief must be something the believer can access by reflection, since justification is a matter of having done well by one's own lights. On the externalist picture, justification can depend on factors outside the believer's ken, such as the reliability of the process that formed the belief.

Luck egalitarians distinguish inequalities that reflect choice from those that reflect brute luck. It is unjust, on this view, for someone to be worse off through no fault of their own, but inequalities flowing from how people freely choose to use equal starting resources are not objectionable. The hard part is drawing the line between chosen and unchosen when choices are shaped by unchosen circumstances.

Critics from the communitarian tradition argue that the language of rights, with its image of separate individuals each shielded by claims, distorts moral life. It crowds out the vocabulary of solidarity, responsibility, and the common good, and pictures society as a truce among strangers rather than a shared life. Defenders reply that rights protect exactly those whom solidarity, in practice, tends to forget.

If mind and body are distinct substances, how does an immaterial decision move a material arm? Causation across the divide seems to require a shared currency the divide rules out. Descartes located the meeting in the pineal gland, but naming a place does not name a mechanism. The interaction problem is not solved by finding where the two substances touch; it is solved only by explaining how they could touch at all.

subtopic: logic and the foundations of inference
sentence: Some propose that the meaning of a logical constant is given by its rules of use, its introduction and elimination rules. This inferentialism faces a famous objection: one could define a connective with rules that license a move from any premise to any conclusion. So not every set of rules confers a coherent meaning, and a criterion is needed to separate the legitimate from the defective.

McTaggart argued that time is unreal. Change requires the A-series, the running of events from future through present to past. But every event is past, present, and future, which is contradictory; and saying it is each at different times presupposes the very series under analysis, launching a regress. The argument is widely rejected, yet no rejection commands consensus.

Underlying these disputes is a question about how richly the world is carved. If composition is unrestricted, there are vastly many objects coinciding everywhere, and the statue puzzle is just one instance. If composition is restricted or denied, the puzzle changes shape. How many things there are in a region is not a question observation answers; it depends on a prior decision about what counts as a thing.

The deprivation account answers Epicurus: death harms by depriving its victim of the goods life would otherwise have contained. The harm is not an experience but a comparative fact, that the person would have been better off had they lived. Death is bad for someone the way a missed inheritance is bad, not by hurting but by subtracting what would have been.

There is a question whether philosophy can deliver wisdom or only analysis. The ancient schools treated philosophy as a way of life, a set of practices for transforming the soul, not merely a body of theory. On the modern academic conception, philosophy is closer to a rigorous discipline of argument. Whether the two can be reunited is itself a live philosophical question.

Defenders reply that the counterintuitive verdicts are the price of taking everyone's welfare seriously, and rival theories pay worse prices elsewhere. A theory that forbids the sacrifice of one to save many must explain why we may let the many die, which can seem its own kind of monstrousness. The dialectic is not utilitarianism versus common sense but a comparison of which deep cost one is willing to bear.

subtopic: power, ideology, and the critique of reason
sentence: Hermeneutical injustice names a wrong done when a group lacks the concepts to make sense of its own experience, because the available interpretive resources were shaped without it. A harm one cannot name is a harm one cannot fully protest. This locates an injustice not in the distribution of goods but in the distribution of the very means of understanding.

Trope theory occupies a middle ground: properties are real but particular, not universal. This redness here and that redness there are two distinct tropes, exactly resembling but numerically different. Sameness of type is then exact resemblance among tropes, and a concrete object is a bundle of tropes. The view trades repeatable universals for a primitive resemblance among particularized qualities.

Objectivism need not claim that moral truths are obvious or that disagreement is irrational. It claims only that there is something disagreement is about, a fact of the matter that makes some moral views better than others. Disagreement, on this view, is not evidence against objectivity but an invitation to inquiry, exactly as in any other domain where reasonable people differ.

How does a name latch onto its bearer? The descriptivist answer is that a name abbreviates a description, and it picks out whoever uniquely satisfies that description. But a speaker can use a name correctly while associating with it a description that is false of the bearer, or true of no one, and that suggests reference is not secured by the descriptions in the speaker's head.
